content: 1. High doses of trimethoprim, renal insufficiency, or concurrent use with other drugs that cause hyperkalemia can significantly increase the risk of hyperkalemia. Serum potassium levels should be closely monitored in these scenarios. 2. Trimethoprim and potassium citrate both elevate serum potassium levels. Caution is advised, and monitoring is necessary when these agents are used together. 3. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia, especially in patients with renal insufficiency, high doses, or when combined with other hyperkalemia-inducing drugs. Close monitoring is essential. 4. Sulfamethoxazole increases the levels of pralatrexate by reducing its renal clearance. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 5. Sulfamethoxazole and pretomanid can mutually increase each other's toxicity. Pretomanid is associated with hepatotoxicity, and co-administration with alcohol, hepatotoxic agents, or certain drugs (excluding bedaquiline and linezolid) should be avoided. Alternative therapies are recommended. 6. Sulfamethoxazole and primaquine may cause hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency due to pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance is unknown, but caution is advised. 7. Sulfamethoxazole levels may be reduced by primidone through hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 8. Probenecid increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 9. Sulfamethoxazole increases procainamide levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Both sulfamethoxazole and procainamide can prolong the QTc interval, necessitating the use of alternative therapies. 10. Prochlorperazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 11. Promazine increases the toxicity of sulfamethoxazole through an unspecified mechanism. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval, and enhanced myelosuppression may occur. Caution and monitoring are required. 12. Promethazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 13. Sulfamethoxazole increases the effects of protamine by decreasing its metabolism and through plasma protein binding competition. Alternative therapies should be considered. 14. Protriptyline and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole may also decrease protriptyline levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 15. Trimethoprim and pyridoxine (vitamin B6) levels may be reduced due to alterations in intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 16. Sulfamethoxazole and pyrimethamine may increase bone marrow toxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Monitoring is advised. 17. Quinidine increases trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. Both drugs prolong the QTc interval, and alternative therapies are recommended. 18. Sulfamethoxazole increases quinine levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 19. Sulfamethoxazole increases ramelteon levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 20. Trimethoprim and ramipril both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitoring is essential. 21. Sulfamethoxazole and ranolazine both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and monitoring are advised. 22. Trimethoprim increases repaglinide levels by decreasing its metabolism. Sulfamethoxazole increases repaglinide levels through plasma protein binding competition. Monitoring is recommended. 23. Trimethoprim increases resmetirom levels by affecting CYP2C8 metabolism. Dose reduction of resmetirom is recommended when co-administered with moderate CYP2C8 inhibitors. 24. Ribociclib increases trimethoprim levels by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 25. Rifabutin decreases trimethoprim levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 26. Rifampin decreases trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme metabolism (CYP3A4 and CYP2C9/10, respectively). The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 27. Sparsentan decreases trimethoprim levels by affecting CYP2C9 metabolism. Sparsentan, a CYP2C9 inducer, reduces the efficacy of CYP2C9 substrates. Monitoring is recommended. 28. Trimethoprim and spironolactone both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitoring is essential. 29. Sulfamethoxazole and spironolactone interact through an unspecified mechanism, increasing sulfamethoxazole levels. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 30. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim both prolong the QTc interval. Monitoring is recommended. 31. Sulfasalazine increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 32. Tafenoquine increases trimethoprim levels by inhibiting organic cation transporter-2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) transporters. Co-administration should be avoided, or substrate-related toxicities should be monitored. 33. Sulfamethoxazole affects tamoxifen metabolism by inhibiting CYP2C9/10, reducing the formation of active metabolites. Monitoring is recommended. 34. Tecovirimat decreases trimethoprim levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Tecovirimat is a weak CYP3A4 inducer, and monitoring of sensitive CYP3A4 substrates is advised. 35. Telavancin and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 36. Trimethoprim and telmisartan both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitoring is essential. 37. Sulfamethoxazole increases terbinafine levels by affecting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 38. Trimethoprim and thiamine levels may be reduced due to alterations in intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 39. Thioridazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 40. Ticlopidine increases sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is recommended. 41. Torsemide increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 42. Trimethoprim increases tovorafenib levels by decreasing its metabolism. Co-administration with strong or moderate CYP2C8 inhibitors should be avoided. 43. Trimethoprim and trandolapril both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitoring is essential. 44. Tranylcypromine increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 45. Trazodone and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole may also decrease trazodone levels through an unspecified mechanism. Monitoring is recommended. 46. Sulfamethoxazole and tretinoin increase phototoxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 47. Trimethoprim and triamterene both increase serum potassium levels. Trimethoprim reduces urinary potassium excretion, which may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitoring is essential. 48. Triamterene increases sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 49. Trifluoperazine and sulfamethoxazole both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 50. Trilaciclib decreases trimethoprim levels by inhibiting OCT2, MATE1, and MATE-2K transporters. Co-administration with substrates where increased concentrations may lead to serious toxicities should be avoided.
